# Cardiac Contractility Modulation Therapy for Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Heart failure (HF) remains a global public health burden, and although guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT), cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT), and implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs) have improved outcomes, a substantial proportion of patients remain symptomatic. Despite the economic burden and large impact on quality of life, substantial effort has focused on multiple medical and device therapies to reduce disease burden and mortality, yet in the past decade only two new medical therapies and no devices had been approved by the US FDA for the treatment of heart failure [1]. Importantly, roughly two-thirds of patients with HF do not meet criteria for CRT, leaving an unmet therapeutic need [1,2]. Cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) emerged to address this gap. CCM is an FDA-approved device-based therapy that delivers biphasic electric stimulation to the ventricular myocardium during the absolute refractory period to augment left ventricular contraction; its benefit is multifactorial, with effects on cellular calcium handling and gene expression leading to regional and global improvement in myocardial contractility without an increase in myocardial oxygen demand [2,3].

## Mechanisms of Action

CCM signals are nonexcitatory, high-amplitude electrical impulses timed to the absolute refractory period, so they cannot trigger a new action potential. CCM signals induce an acute, mild augmentation of left ventricular contractile strength without an increase in myocardial oxygen consumption in both animal HF models and patients with reduced ejection fraction [4]. Preclinical canine studies established the structural and molecular basis: therapy with CCM electrical signals improves left ventricular function and remodeling in dogs with chronic heart failure [5]. At the cellular level, improved calcium handling (phosphorylation of phospholamban, upregulation of SERCA-2A), reversal of the fetal myocyte gene program associated with heart failure, and reverse remodeling are observed [1]. In patients, CCM electrical signals improve myocardial gene expression in heart failure [6]. CCM also normalizes calcium-handling proteins, including expression and phosphorylation of the Na⁺-Ca²⁺ exchanger and calcium-binding proteins delivered to LV muscle during the absolute refractory period, improving LV function [7,8]. These mechanisms distinguish CCM from cyclic-AMP–dependent inotropes that increase oxygen demand and mortality.

## Clinical Evidence

The first randomized study, FIX-HF-4, was a double-blind, double-crossover European trial. In this randomized, double-blind, crossover study, 164 subjects with EF < 35% and NYHA class II or III symptoms received a CCM pulse generator, demonstrating improvements in peak VO₂ and quality of life [9]. The subsequent US FIX-HF-5 trial randomized 428 patients. CCM was tested in 428 NYHA class III/IV, narrow-QRS HF patients with EF ≤ 35%; the primary safety endpoint was a noninferiority test between groups at 12 months for the composite of all-cause mortality and hospitalizations [10]. The overall primary efficacy endpoint was not met, but a subgroup with EF 25–45% derived benefit, prompting FIX-HF-5C [11]. In FIX-HF-5C, 160 patients with NYHA III/IV symptoms, QRS < 130 ms, and EF 25–45% were randomized to medical therapy or CCM for 24 weeks; CCM was safe, improved exercise tolerance and quality of life, and led to fewer HF hospitalizations [12]. A simplified system was later validated: the 2-lead system effectively delivers comparable CCM signals as the 3-lead system, is equally safe, improves peak VO₂ and NYHA class, with fewer device-related adverse effects [13].

A patient-level meta-analysis strengthened these findings. In 2020, Giallauria et al performed a comprehensive individual patient data meta-analysis of randomized trials plus FIX-HF-5C2 including 861 patients, and pooled analysis showed CCM significantly improved peak VO₂, 6-minute walk distance, and quality of life [14]. An earlier individual-patient meta-analysis reported consistent improvements in exercise capacity and quality of life [15].

## Real-World and Long-Term Data

Registry data extend follow-up beyond clinical trials. CCM-REG, a prospective registry of 503 patients from 51 European centres, found CCM improved functional status, quality of life, and LVEF, reduced HF hospitalization rates compared with prior history, and survival at 1 and 3 years was significantly better than predicted by the MAGGIC risk score [16]. Anker et al reported that CCM improves long-term survival and hospitalizations in HF with reduced ejection fraction [17]. An earlier 2-year registry found that over 2 years there were eighteen deaths (7 cardiovascular), with overall survival of 86.4% [18]. A case-control analysis found that CCM resulted in significant improvement of long-term survival, particularly in those with EF 25–40%, with a reduction in HF hospitalizations in patients with less severely reduced EF [19]. Contemporary mid-term cohort data corroborate improvements in NYHA class and cardiac function [20]. Procedurally, the implant resembles pacemaker placement, and implantation of right ventricular electrodes for CCM did not worsen tricuspid regurgitation in patients with HFrEF [21,22].

## Patient Selection and Emerging Directions

Current evidence best supports CCM in symptomatic HFrEF patients ineligible for CRT. Collectively, prior randomized studies indicated CCM improves functional class, quality of life, and exercise tolerance, particularly in patients with LVEF 25–45%, NYHA III symptoms despite GDMT, normal QRS duration, and sinus rhythm [23,24]. Investigation is extending toward broader populations. A pilot study (CCM-HFpEF) demonstrated that the benefits of CCM may extend to the HFpEF population, with significant improvement in health status and no obvious safety impact [25,26], and the AIM HIGHer trial is evaluating CCM in HFmrEF and HFpEF [27]. A next-generation device combining CCM with defibrillator functionality (CCM-D) is being evaluated in the prospective, single-arm INTEGRA-D study, enrolling 300 stage C/D HF patients with LVEF ≤ 40% for whom de novo ICD is indicated [28,29].

## Limitations and Conclusion

CCM offers a mechanistically distinct, well-tolerated option for selected symptomatic HF patients. However, the strongest evidence relates to functional capacity and quality-of-life outcomes, whereas large randomized trials powered for hard clinical endpoints remain limited, and much long-term data derive from observational registries subject to residual confounding [30]. Adequately powered, blinded, parallel-design randomized trials are needed to define effects on mortality and morbidity before broader adoption.
